id: More than one man has reached up my skirt

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I’ve stopped asking: ¿Why? I’ve let a man whistle from the table for more beer, & brought it to him with a smile. I’ve slapped a man & ran while he laughed — atrevida. I’ve had a miscarriage. I’ve let a man kiss me after an abortion & comforted his hot tears. I’ve done these things, while other girls work in maquilas piecing together Dell computer boards, while other girls work in brothels, & cake foundation across their bruised arms, while other girls ride the bus home alone at night, every night, while other girls are found wearing clothes that don’t belong to them, or no clothes at all. I’ve done all of this while other girls are found with puta written in blood across their broken bellies. My mother used to cover my eyes when we’d walk by girls working the corner, & say: See how lucky you are,not to have to work like they do? I have been muy puta, have been called puta.Yes, I’d say, very lucky.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Why, Dell, See

outputs.L1: I’ve stopped asking, ¿Why? I’ve let a man whistle from his table for more beer and brought it to him with a smile. I’ve slapped a man and run while he laughed—atrevida. I’ve had a miscarriage. I’ve let a man kiss me after an abortion and comforted his hot tears. outputs.L2:
I no longer ask, “Why?” I have allowed a man to summon me from his table with a whistle when he wanted another beer, and I carried it over to him smiling. I have hit a man and then taken off running as he laughed and called me atrevida. I have lost a pregnancy. I have permitted a man to kiss me after an abortion and have soothed him while his face burned with tears.

I have lived through these things while other girls labor in maquilas, assembling Dell computer boards piece by piece; while other girls are in brothels, spreading thick foundation over the bruises on their arms; while other girls take the bus back by themselves in the dark, night after night; while other girls are discovered dressed in clothes that are not theirs, or wearing nothing at all. I have done all this while other girls are found with puta written in blood across their battered stomachs.

When I was young, my mother would shield my eyes as we passed girls standing on the corner and tell me, “Look how fortunate you are, not having to work the way they do.” I have been muy puta. I have been called puta.

“Yes,” I would answer. “Very fortunate.”
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on a history of enduring degrading and painful experiences involving men, but she no longer asks why these things happened to her. Instead of searching for explanations, she seems to recognize these experiences as part of a broader pattern of violence and humiliation directed at women. Her tone suggests exhaustion, resignation, and a painful awareness that such treatment is not isolated or accidental.

At the same time, she contrasts her own suffering with the even harsher realities faced by other girls and women. She thinks of girls working in factories, where their labor may be exploited; girls trapped in brothels, where their bodies are treated as commodities; and girls forced to survive on unsafe streets, exposed to danger and abuse. This comparison does not erase her own pain, but it places it within a wider social context. The speaker understands that many women live under conditions that are even more brutal and precarious than her own.

The text also emphasizes the different forms of violence women experience. This violence can be physical, leaving bruises on women’s bodies. It can be fatal, ending in murder. It can also be social and verbal, as women are publicly shamed and reduced to the word “puta.” The insult becomes a weapon used to control, degrade, and punish women, especially those judged for their sexuality or their perceived failure to conform to expectations of respectability.

The speaker remembers how her mother once framed sex workers as women who were less fortunate. Her mother taught her to see herself as lucky by comparison, as someone spared from the worst forms of exploitation and disgrace. This lesson reflects a survival strategy: by pointing to women who seemed to suffer more, the mother encouraged her daughter to feel grateful for her own circumstances.

However, the speaker complicates this idea of luck. She recognizes that, even if she has not lived the exact same life as the women her mother described, she has still been sexualized, judged, and humiliated. She, too, has been looked at through the lens of male desire and social condemnation. She, too, has been called “puta.” In this way, the speaker challenges the simple division between “lucky” and “unlucky” women, showing that misogyny and sexual shame affect women across different situations. Her reflection reveals that the boundaries between respectability and disgrace are fragile, and that no woman is fully protected from the violence of being reduced, judged, or named by others.
outputs.L4:
The text explores gendered exploitation, shame, and survival through a first-person speaker who reflects on her own experiences while also bearing witness to the suffering of other girls and women. The speaker does not present her pain as isolated or exceptional; instead, she places it within a wider pattern of violence, judgment, and social indifference. By cataloging stories of labor, abuse, sexualization, and murder, the text shows how women’s bodies are repeatedly treated as objects to be used, blamed, or discarded. The speaker’s voice becomes both personal and collective, moving between her individual memories and the broader reality of women whose lives have been marked by danger.

A central tension in the text is the idea of “luck.” At first, survival might appear to be a form of good fortune, but the text complicates that idea by showing how bitter and limited such luck really is. To be “lucky” in this world may simply mean not being killed, not being assaulted in a particular moment, or not being punished as severely as someone else. This kind of luck does not suggest safety or justice; it reveals how low the expectations for women’s survival have become. The speaker recognizes that her continued life is a privilege when compared with the fates of other women, but that privilege is deeply uncomfortable. Her survival does not free her from shame, fear, or memory. Instead, it forces her to confront the systems that make survival seem accidental.

The text also examines how shame is imposed on women rather than on those who harm them. Girls and women are judged for their bodies, their sexuality, their poverty, their labor, and even their victimhood. They are expected to carry the burden of violence committed against them, while the larger culture often excuses or ignores the people and institutions responsible. Through this critique, the speaker exposes a world in which women are constantly made vulnerable and then blamed for that vulnerability.

Ultimately, the text presents survival as both a personal fact and a political accusation. The speaker has lived, but her survival does not resolve the violence around her. Instead, it highlights the cruelty of a society in which some women survive while others are exploited, abused, or murdered. By linking her own experiences to the experiences of others, the speaker transforms private pain into a broader indictment of systemic gendered violence. The text insists that survival should not depend on luck, and that a world in which it does is profoundly unjust.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem in a Latina/Chicana voice about survival, misogyny, sex work, abortion, and femicide, blending English and Spanish and using repetition around the idea of being “lucky.”
counterfactuals.output:
They tell me I’m lucky.

Lucky, porque I came home before sunrise with both shoes on, with my mouth still mine, with my name not folded into a police report. Lucky because the car slowed but did not stop. Lucky because the man paid, lucky because the man left, lucky because the man only called me puta and not cadáver. Lucky, mija, lucky.

But what is luck when it is just the thin wall between my body and the world’s hunger?

I learned early that survival has many names: rent, lipstick, fake smile, cab fare, clinic, lie. I learned to count money in the bathroom stall, to tuck bills into my bra like little saints. San Dólar, ruega por nosotras. I learned the difference between a man looking and a man hunting. I learned how to laugh with my teeth showing so they would think I was not afraid. I learned fear could be a perfume, dulce and metallic, clinging to the throat.

They tell me I’m lucky.

Lucky I had a cousin who knew a nurse who knew a place. Lucky I crossed town with my hoodie up, past the women praying outside, past the signs with dead babies and no dead mothers. Lucky I bled and kept bleeding and did not die. Lucky the body can be a house you burn down and rebuild, burn down and rebuild. Lucky I chose myself when everyone said choosing myself was a sin.

Ay, but they never call the men sinful when they leave their fingerprints inside our lives.

They call us girls, mujeres, mothers, temptations, evidence. They call us too loud, too brown, too broken, too much. They call us missing when we have been taken. They call us found when only bones come back. They say she was alone, she was drinking, she was selling, she was walking, she was asking for it, she was no angel.

As if angels are the only ones allowed to live.

I say her name and another name rises behind it. I say hermana and the street fills with candles. I say ni una más and still, another mother tears the night apart with her hands. The border is a mouth full of teeth. The city is a locked door. The desert keeps secrets, but not because it wants to. The river carries what men throw away.

They tell me I’m lucky.

Lucky my father only shouted. Lucky my boyfriend only shoved. Lucky the cop only laughed. Lucky the judge only frowned. Lucky the client only wanted to talk about his wife. Lucky the pill worked. Lucky the blood stopped. Lucky the bruises bloomed where sleeves could hide them. Lucky I was born stubborn, lengua filosa, corazón de nopal—cut me and I grow spines.

Pero escúchame: I am not lucky like a coin tossed into a fountain. I am lucky like a blade found in the grass. I am lucky like a match in a blackout. I am lucky because my abuela whispered, corre, and my mother whispered, aguanta, and my own body whispered, todavía.

Still.

Still I wake. Still I paint my mouth red, not for beauty, but for war. Still I love women who know the price of being alive. Still I carry condoms, pepper spray, misoprostol prayers, the phone numbers of girls who answer at 3 a.m. Still I know which men to flatter, which streets to avoid, which rooms have windows. Still I dance when the cumbia comes on, because joy is also a weapon, cabrones, and I have not surrendered mine.

They tell me I’m lucky.

No. I am practiced.

I am the daughter of women who turned hunger into tortillas, grief into gossip, shame into gold hoops shining at the laundromat. I am the sister of the missing, the working, the bleeding, the choosing, the buried, the still-here. I am every “cuidado” text sent and answered. I am every key between the fingers. I am every body the world tried to make disposable, standing in the mirror saying, no me mataron.

Lucky?

Maybe.

Lucky like a weed through concrete. Lucky like a scar that closed. Lucky like the girl who came home, yes, but also like the girl who didn’t—and whose name I carry under my tongue, una flor, una furia, una promesa.

I am lucky because I survived.

I am angry because I had to.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a raw first-person literary monologue from a young woman near the U.S.–Mexico border reflecting on violence against women, maquilas, shame, and being called “puta.”
counterfactuals.output:
They call me *puta* like they’re spitting out a seed.

Like the word was already in their mouths before I walked by. Like it was waiting for my hips, my skirt, my lipstick, my silence. Like my body is a public wall and anybody with a dirty hand can write on it.

*Puta.*

Sometimes they say it laughing. Sometimes from a truck. Sometimes a man old enough to be my father says it soft, almost sweet, like he’s offering me a flower made of rot. Sometimes a woman says it too, under her breath, because shame is a language we learned from our mothers and their mothers, passed down with recipes and prayers and warnings: don’t walk there, don’t wear that, don’t answer back, don’t be alone, don’t be seen, don’t disappear.

As if disappearing is something we do on purpose.

Here, near the border, everything is always crossing or waiting to cross. Trucks, money, bodies, rumors, ghosts. The desert keeps secrets badly. It gives them back in pieces: a shoe, a braid, a name nobody wants to print correctly. The factories glow all night, maquilas humming like metal insects, swallowing girls before dawn and coughing them out after dark with their backs bent, fingers sore, eyes full of fluorescent light.

My cousin worked in one.

I say “worked” because that is the official word. She worked. She clocked in. She assembled wires for things she would never own. She packed parts for machines going north, where people touch buttons and never wonder whose hands made them possible. She wore her hair tied up. She carried pepper spray. She called her mother when she left the line. She knew the rules. All of us know the rules.

Still.

That word sits in the mouth like a stone.

Still, she didn’t come home.

And after, people became very careful with their pity. They lowered their voices. They asked questions that were not questions. What time did she leave? Was she alone? Did she have a boyfriend? Was she seeing someone? Did she drink? Did she fight with anybody? What was she wearing?

What was she wearing.

As if a blouse can summon a grave. As if denim can sign a death sentence. As if a girl’s laughter is a door she leaves unlocked.

They called her *muchacha* when she was useful, *señorita* when she was quiet, *puta* when she was gone.

I want to tear that word open with my teeth.

I want to ask them what they call the men who wait in cars. What they call the bosses who look too long. What they call the police who lose papers, the judges who lose time, the newspapers that lose interest, the city that loses women and keeps building parking lots over its own memory.

I want to know why shame always finds us first.

Before the ambulance. Before the report. Before the candlelight vigil with the white balloons and the mothers holding photographs in plastic sleeves so the rain won’t touch their daughters’ faces. Shame arrives early. Shame sits in the kitchen. Shame folds its hands and says, *maybe if.*

Maybe if she had taken another route. Maybe if she had stayed home. Maybe if she had been less pretty, less friendly, less tired, less poor. Maybe if she had been born somewhere else, with a different passport, a different street, a different God.

Maybe if she had been a son.

My mother says not to talk like this. She says words can bring trouble. I tell her trouble is already here. It eats breakfast with us. It rides the bus. It stands outside the maquila gates and watches the girls pour out in blue uniforms, all of them pretending not to be afraid because fear is expensive. Fear makes you late. Fear makes you weak. Fear makes your hands shake when the supervisor is already saying faster, faster, faster.

The border teaches you that your body has a price even when you are not selling it.

A wage is a price. A bribe is a price. A ransom is a price. A silence is a price. A rumor is a price. A woman’s life becomes a number people argue about. How many missing, how many dead, how many counted twice, how many never counted at all. Numbers lined up like crosses. Numbers neat enough to make horror look organized.

But I remember my cousin messy.

I remember her eating mango with chile and getting it all over her fingers. I remember her singing badly and loudly. I remember her cussing at the television. I remember her asleep on our sofa with one sock missing. I remember the little scar on her chin from falling off a bicycle when we were kids. I remember her saying she was saving money to study beauty, maybe open a salon, maybe paint nails with tiny flowers, maybe get out, maybe stay but in a better house, maybe buy her mother a washing machine so her hands would stop cracking in winter.

She was not a lesson.

She was not a warning.

She was not a girl-shaped mistake.

And I am so tired of how they turn dead women into advice for living ones.

Don’t go out.

Don’t trust men.

Don’t trust women either.

Don’t trust taxis.

Don’t trust buses.

Don’t trust the police.

Don’t trust the dark.

Don’t trust your own wanting.

Don’t want.

That is what they mean. Strip yourself down to survival. Become smaller than danger. Fold yourself into a saint, a shadow, a locked room. And even then, if violence comes through the wall, they will ask why you built the wall there.

Sometimes I feel shame rise in me for no reason. I’ll be standing in line at the store, or washing my hair, or laughing with my friends, and suddenly it crawls up my throat. Shame that I have a body. Shame that men look. Shame that sometimes I like being looked at before I remember what looking can become. Shame that I am alive when others are not. Shame that I cross streets quickly. Shame that I hold my keys between my fingers. Shame that I still want red lipstick.

But I do.

I want red lipstick. I want music. I want to dance without calculating the exits. I want to walk home under a sky full of stars and think only that the stars are beautiful, not that the desert is wide enough to hide anything. I want to wear what I want and not have my clothes dragged into court as witnesses against me. I want to be kissed and not condemned for having a mouth.

They say *puta* because they are afraid of a woman who belongs to herself.

They say it to put a fence around us. But I live near fences. I know they are never only there to keep people out. They are there to keep people cheap. To keep them desperate. To decide who is a worker and who is illegal, who is a victim and who is guilty, who is mourned and who is forgotten.

The maquilas taught the city how to use women up and call it opportunity.

Come, they said. There is work for your small hands. Come, they said. You are better than men for this, more patient, more obedient. Come stand all day under white lights. Come breathe dust. Come earn just enough to return tomorrow. Come be grateful. Come be replaceable.

And when the women began to vanish, the city shrugged like a man pretending his hands are clean.

But our mothers did not shrug.

They searched.

With flyers, with photographs, with plastic bags full of water and bread, with rosaries wrapped around their fists. They searched places no one wanted to search. They learned the names of roads, ditches, canals, empty lots. They stood in offices where men made them wait. They shouted until their voices broke. They became difficult. Crazy. Bitter. Unfeminine.

Good.

Let grief become unfeminine.

Let rage grow a mustache and spit on the floor.

Let every mother’s cry crack the windows of the courthouse.

I used to think being called *puta* stained me. I used to feel the word land on my skin and burn. I would go home and scrub my arms, my neck, the back of my knees, as if insult had a smell. I would hear it again in bed. *Puta.* Like a fly in the dark.

Now I think the shame belongs elsewhere.

Let it crawl back to the mouths that made it. Let it sit on the tongues of men who confuse hunger with power. Let it stain the uniforms of officers who laugh. Let it cling to factory owners who count profit under portraits of saints. Let it sleep beside politicians who visit mothers only when cameras are near. Let it rot in the churches that preach purity louder than justice.

I am not pure.

I am not dirty either.

I am a girl with dust on my shoes from a city that keeps burying its daughters and calling the ground empty.

I am alive, and that is not an apology.

When they call me *puta* now, I turn around. Not always. I am not stupid. I know a brave woman can become a dead woman. I know pride does not stop a knife. But sometimes, when the street is bright enough, when there are people nearby, when my anger is bigger than my fear, I turn around and look straight at them.

I make them see my face.

Not a body passing. Not a rumor. Not a thing to name and throw away.

A face.

A witness.

A border.

A warning.

My name is not *puta*. My cousin’s name was not *puta*. The missing have names. The murdered have names. The women on the line have names. The girls at the bus stop at five in the morning, hugging themselves against the cold, have names. We carry them like contraband across every checkpoint of silence.

And if this city has taught me anything, it is that silence is another factory.

It takes in women and produces ghosts.

So I speak. Even with my voice shaking. Even with my mother crying in the next room. Even with men laughing. Even with the word waiting in their mouths.

Let them say it.

I know what I am.

I am the daughter of women who searched the desert.

I am the friend of women who work nights.

I am the cousin of a girl whose photograph refuses to fade.

I am the body they tried to shame into obedience.

I am still here.

And I am not ashamed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a brief, emotionally intense piece of hybrid poetry/prose that juxtaposes personal trauma with the murders and exploitation of other women, using code-switching and an accusatory tone.
counterfactuals.output:
You call it history. I call it a room with no doors.

Mi madre said, *no mires*, don’t look—  
but the world kept holding up women like evidence:  
their names peeled off by headlines,  
their bodies turned into warnings,  
their labor folded into clean sheets for someone else’s bed.

And you—sí, tú—  
you asked why I flinch.

As if my fear were born alone.  
As if it did not arrive with sisters:  
the girl in the alley, the woman in the factory,  
la migrante with her wages stolen,  
the wife buried under “private matters,”  
the dead renamed “statistics” before their blood was dry.

You built a country out of our bruises  
and called it civilization.

I carry my own wound in my mouth,  
but when I speak, it becomes a choir—  
not gentle, not grateful, not yours to edit.

Listen:  
every silence you demanded  
has been learning your name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write in the style of contemporary confessional borderlands poetry: a speaker lists painful experiences with men while comparing her life to girls in factories, brothels, buses, and on the streets.
counterfactuals.output:
**Inventory at the Border**

I have been a girl  
with my name folded small  
under a man’s tongue.

I have been asked to smile  
at the checkpoint,  
at the kitchen table,  
in the back seat where the locks  
clicked down like teeth.

I have learned the weight  
of a hand on my wrist—  
how it can become a country,  
how it can make a room  
need passports.

There are girls in factories  
sewing blue jeans for women  
who will never know  
the needle entered first  
through brown light,  
through hunger,  
through a thumb wrapped in tape.

I think of them  
when a man calls me *mija*  
and means *mine*.  
When he says he loves me  
like a foreman loves overtime.

There are girls in brothels  
painting their mouths red  
as exit signs,  
counting bills with faces  
of dead presidents  
who never learned their names.

I think of them  
when a man leaves money  
on the dresser  
for the taxi,  
for silence,  
for me to understand  
what kind of mercy  
he believes he has given.

There are girls on buses  
sleeping with one eye open,  
their knees pressed together  
like a prayer  
no saint has answered.

I think of them  
when the man beside me  
spreads himself wide  
as a border wall,  
as if my body is the land  
he was promised  
by a god with his voice.

There are girls on streets  
selling oranges, gum, roses,  
their shadows long and thin  
under the headlights.

I think of them  
when men slow down  
to ask how much  
for what was never for sale—  
my walk, my laugh,  
the heat I carry  
from one city to another.

I have mistaken attention  
for shelter.  
I have called a locked door  
a home.  
I have kissed men  
who tasted like beer, dust,  
and my own disappearance.

Once, a man told me  
I was lucky  
to be wanted.

I looked at the river  
dragging the moon  
in pieces across its back.  
I looked at the bridge,  
all those headlights  
trying to become stars.

Lucky is a word  
men use  
when they survive themselves.

I am still here,  
which is not the same  
as being whole.

But tonight  
I gather my names  
from under every boot,  
from every motel sheet,  
from every factory siren,  
every bus window,  
every corner where a girl  
learned to become stone  
without losing her pulse.

I press them to my chest.

I say:  
this body is not a border  
you may cross.

This mouth is not a wound  
for you to enter.

This life—  
stitched, sold, watched, followed—  
is still mine.

And mine  
is a country  
I am learning  
to defend.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark feminist prose poem about a mother telling her daughter she is lucky not to be a prostitute, while the daughter reflects on abortion, abuse, and violence against women.
counterfactuals.output:
My mother says I am lucky I am not a prostitute, and the word falls from her mouth like a coin dropped into a well: small, hard, disappearing. She says it while folding towels, as if luck is a clean thing, as if a woman’s life can be stacked into white squares and put away.

I want to ask her what luck means in a house where silence learned to wear my name. What luck means when men are called storms and we are called weathered. When a girl is taught to count exits before she counts stars. When her body becomes a country everyone has an opinion about, a border argued over by fathers, judges, husbands, strangers with holy books in their hands and hunger in their eyes.

I think of the child I did not become a mother to. The small possible future I released back into darkness. How they called it murder, but never named the hands already around my throat. Never named the rooms where girls are cornered into motherhood, then blamed for the crying. Never named the men who plant fear and walk away clean.

My mother says I am lucky, and I look at her wrists, thin as unfinished sentences. I know she is speaking from the old country of survival, where women bless the cage if the door is not locked from the outside. She means: no man has bought you by the hour. She means: no one sees the price you paid.

But I have been purchased in other currencies. With shame. With obedience. With the terror of being believed too late. I have paid in blood, in sleep, in the soft animal of my own wanting. I have paid to keep breathing.

Outside, the world sharpens itself on women. Another body in an alley. Another daughter missing. Another headline washed clean of the word hatred. Another man described as lonely, troubled, promising. Another woman described by what she wore, what she drank, why she stayed, why she left, why she did not scream loud enough to wake God.

My mother says I am lucky I am not a prostitute.

I say nothing.

In my silence, all the dead women sit down beside me. The unloved. The used. The disbelieved. The ones who sold what the world had already stolen. The ones who never sold anything and were still taken. We pass a dark bread from hand to hand. We eat. We are not grateful. We are not clean. We are not ashamed.

We are only alive, which is not the same as lucky.

And somewhere inside me, a daughter I will never have opens her eyes and learns the first lesson of womanhood: that even mercy comes with a mouthful of blame, and even mothers sometimes hand you the knife by its blade.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
